grammar.explanation: This pattern gives a reason or cause. After a noun or a nominal adjective, it follows the linking form ending in na.
This pattern describes an action continuing from the past toward the present, or movement toward the speaker's location.
This pattern introduces a term as the topic of a definition or explanation.
This pattern reports a generally held view or description, meaning is said to. The simple passive form can serve the same reporting function.
This pattern lists representative actions without implying that the list is exhaustive. Each listed action counts as one occurrence.
This pattern is a written-style negative connection meaning without doing. It may be followed by ni.
This pattern means even without doing something, showing that the result holds despite the action's absence.
This pattern makes an event or situation the topic and then explains its cause: the reason something happens is that.
This pattern expresses a change in ability, habit, or state: becoming able to do something or beginning to do it regularly.
This pattern means doing something in preparation or leaving the resulting state in place.
This pattern introduces a condition or a completed prerequisite, meaning if or when. Here it marks when to take the next cooking step.
This pattern follows a dictionary-form verb and expresses ability or possibility.
This pattern adds another quality or fact, meaning not only but also.
This pattern marks the role, status, or category in which something is regarded, meaning as.
This pattern combines a verb's volitional form with an attempt or intention to perform the action.
This pattern attaches to a verb stem to describe something as easy to do. Here it describes food as easy or agreeable to eat.
This pattern describes an action or change developing onward over time.
This pattern states that someone has never had a particular experience. In the past tense, it means had never done something before that time.
This pattern expresses movement toward the speaker or a change developing over time up to the point being described.
This pattern attaches to a verb stem to mean that an action is easy to do.
This pattern reports a generally accepted statement or explanation, meaning that something is said to be the case.
This pattern describes a change in habitual behavior or ability: someone begins doing something or becomes able to do it.
This pattern lists representative activities without presenting an exhaustive list.
This pattern turns an action into a noun-like expression so it can be discussed as an activity or occurrence.
This pattern introduces the reason or cause for the following statement.
This pattern links a condition or event to a natural consequence, often meaning when or once.
This pattern expresses carrying an action forward or movement away; it can describe proceeding with an examination or taking something along.
This pattern identifies a time or situation associated with a noun, here the occasions when bread or rice is eaten.
This pattern poses a reflective or explanatory question, inviting the reader to consider what the answer might be.
This pattern expresses the ability or opportunity to perform an action. Context distinguishes it from passive forms with similar endings.
This pattern presents the subject as receiving an action, as when food is sold or prepared; the person performing it may be omitted.
This pattern connects an adjective to another description, often corresponding to and.
This pattern means to be known for doing something. A plain-form verb names the activity for which someone is known.
This pattern says that an action happens often. Replacing the subject marker with the additive marker includes it among other frequent actions.
This pattern means although or even though and often conveys surprise that the following situation contradicts expectations.
This pattern links two nouns to show that the second is intended for the first, such as food intended for a particular occasion.
This pattern expresses doing something in advance for a later purpose. Its past form describes preparation already completed.
This pattern expresses prohibition: an action must not be done.
This pattern expresses a desired result or purpose, meaning so that. It often follows a potential verb describing what someone will be able to do.
This pattern describes a change into a new habit or state, meaning to begin doing something or to come to do it.
This pattern reports a generally held statement or belief, meaning it is said that. Its continuing-state form emphasizes that the statement is commonly repeated.
This pattern attaches to a verb stem to express continuing to perform an action or continuing to undergo a change.
This pattern introduces a comparison, meaning compared with. The preceding noun supplies the comparison standard.
This pattern follows a verb's negative form to express a change in which an action stops happening or becomes less customary.
This pattern means instead of or in place of the preceding noun.
This pattern lists representative actions without claiming to list every possibility. It can also use a single listed action before the sentence continues.
This pattern asks a reflective or gently phrased question about an explanation or uncertain situation. After a noun predicate, an additional linking syllable is required.
This pattern singles out a term as the topic of a definition or explanation, often asking what it really means.
